meta.title: The turbulent AI era is here
meta.author: aryeh

comments.author: Levitating
comments.text:
AI will either be the greatest equalizer ever invented, or the worst source of injustice.


It's easy to take two opposing extremes like this and state the outcome will be one or the other. Makes for a powerful quote that's hard to prove wrong.

comments.author: aryeh
comments.text:
I think Bill Gates is almost uniquely positioned to offer a perspective on AI worth considering. One statement particularly hit home for me :-


The biggest shift for workers will happen when AI provides nearly error-free work. At that point, it will be able to function on its own without a human checking in on it, and companies will have every economic incentive to let it.

comments.author: nemin
comments.text: That "when" should be a big "if" instead.

comments.author: tao_oat
comments.text: One could say the same for human work.

comments.author: lpil
comments.text: The difference being that humans already exist, so there's no requirement for us to create new data centres etc to produce them.

comments.author: shonfeder
comments.text: And we don't need to justify their existence by being useful enough to produce, because they are sources of value and meaning, not production machines!

comments.author: lpil
comments.text: Yeah exactly. I find many of the comparisons online between humans and machines distasteful for this reason.

comments.author: Levitating
comments.text:
I am immediately reminded of this Sam Altman quote:

"One of the things that's always unfair in this comparison, is people compare the energy it takes to train an AI model, to the energy it takes a human run an inference query. But it also takes a lot to train a human, it takes like 20 years and a lot of food you eat during that time before you get smart."1

I can't believe the follow-up question to this wasn't whether Sam believes a grown human has the same value to society as an AI model. The concept of valueing a human based on produce is disgusting.

comments.author: shonfeder
comments.text:
Absolutely. When you listen to these people talk, they have a clearly undeveloped or degenerated moral intelligence. They do not understand basic precepts of reasoning about ethics, or how to think about the value and meaning of human lives. I honestly doubt that they could articulate the basic premises of vulgar utilitarianism, which is the most idiotic of modern ethical frameworks, without being prepped for it.

My working hypothesis is that this is because they are not actually functioning as sapient subjects: they are so wired into the techno-capital machine that they are essentially roboticized -- cogs in the system. They happen to be cogs in a directive unit, but they are cogs nevertheless. You can see this too in their surrender of agency, they will literally say that they are just following the unfolding flow of the system and don't know where it's going etc., or that there are no other options, because this course is inevitable etc.

comments.author: tao_oat
comments.text: I mean, that is true, but I'm not sure what your argument is! Human hands already exist, so there's really no need for us to create tools, etc., yet there are obvious benefits to doing so.

comments.author: lpil
comments.text:
My statement was that the cost of the current approach to AI is extremely high, and there's no additional cost to humans having jobs, so your suggested human-AI equivalence doesn't seem very robust.

Almost all other tools are inexpensive compared to AI, so that comparison doesn't seem to work either.

comments.author: Levitating
comments.text: Your argument isn't clear to me either. nemin argued that error-free work provided by AI isn't a given. How does human work related to that?

comments.author: flaviusb
comments.text: I mean, the rate is meaningfully different though, right? Like, on any serious look, AI is about a million times more 'error-y' than a human worker (as eg most humans go their entire career without making the kinds of severe mistakes that AI makes pretty regularly), with no path to get better, no real acknowledgement of the current status of the thing just 'but what if in the future it's good thought, therefore it will be good in the future, therefore it counts as good now'...

comments.author: tao_oat
comments.text:
There are definitely many things that I would not trust an AI to do today! But also many (and increasing) tasks where AIs outperform humans. (e.g. https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.adz4433)

But if you look at the trajectory of what kind of tasks they can handle, the trend is pretty clear, isn't it? I'm thinking of e.g. METR's time horizon work at https://metr.org/time-horizons

comments.author: bediger4000
comments.text: One could, but humans exist now, can be studied, and we can find categories of errors. We can make aids to help (LSP servers, syntax features in programming languages, ASLR) the categories of errors. We don't expect most people to do error-free work, and our cognitive biases prevent us from treating them as demigods. "AI", on the other hand, seems to have some underlying problems that prevent aids from helping. Additionally, human cognitive biases make "The AI said it" into something like a conversation stopping cliche. The bias towards accepting authoritatively-stated answers that appear correct, but contain errors, makes an unpredictably-erroneous AI into something dangerous. If we're going to accept AI answers as definitive or authoritative, as we all have a bias to do, the AI must be nearly error-free.
